claims.evidence: This is inferred from the metagene analysis and illustrated in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Large footprints extend 10 nt beyond the A-site codon.
claims.source: Using this as a reference for phasing all the footprints, we inferred that for ribosomes with a given codon in the A site, small and large footprints generally had the same 5′ ends positioned 15–16 nt upstream of the A-site codon, and differed at their 3′ ends: extending 2–3 nt beyond the A-site codon in the small footprints and 10 nt beyond the A-site codon in the large footprints, respectively (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the metagene analysis and illustrated in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: The non-rotated, pre-peptide-bond ribosomes and rotated, post-peptide-bond ribosomes might protect different lengths of mRNA.
claims.source: We hypothesized that the non-rotated, pre-peptide-bond ribosomes and rotated, post-peptide-bond ribosomes might protect different lengths of mRNA, and that the two resulting footprint sizes might, therefore, represent these two conformations.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claims.claim: The two footprint sizes might represent non-rotated and rotated ribosome conformations.
claims.source: We hypothesized that the non-rotated, pre-peptide-bond ribosomes and rotated, post-peptide-bond ribosomes might protect different lengths of mRNA, and that the two resulting footprint sizes might, therefore, represent these two conformations.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claims.claim: Cycloheximide is an elongation inhibitor that binds to the E site of ribosomes, preventing the E site tRNA from leaving the ribosome.
claims.source: Cycloheximide is an elongation inhibitor that binds to the E site of ribosomes, preventing the E site tRNA from leaving the ribosome.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about cycloheximide's mechanism of action.

claims.claim: When cycloheximide was added to yeast, the most prevalent footprints were 28–30 nt long and were distributed along the coding sequence with a 3-nt periodicity.
claims.source: When cycloheximide was added to the yeast immediately before harvest and was present throughout lysis and RNase I treatment, the most prevalent footprints were 28–30 nt long and were distributed along the coding sequence with a 3-nt periodicity (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: In the presence of cycloheximide, there were very few 20–22 nt footprints apart from a distinct peak at the start codon.
claims.source: Apart from a distinct peak at the start codon, there were very few 20–22 nt footprints.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Cycloheximide stabilizes one stage of the elongation cycle.
claims.source: Our data confirmed previous evidence that the ribosome predominantly protects a 28 nt footprint in the presence of cycloheximide, and suggest that cycloheximide stabilizes one stage of the elongation cycle.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the predominance of 28 nt footprints with cycloheximide treatment.

claims.claim: Cycloheximide bound alongside a tRNA in the E site prevents either the incorporation of the next aminoacylated tRNA in the A site or peptide bond formation.
claims.source: Previous work shows that cycloheximide bound alongside a tRNA in the E site prevents either the incorporation of the next aminoacylated tRNA in the A site or peptide bond formation (Schneider-Poetsch et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Cycloheximide is expected to trap the ribosome in a non-rotated conformation.
claims.source: In either case, it is expected to trap the ribosome in a non-rotated conformation, suggesting that the non-rotated conformation protects 28–30 nt of mRNA.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism of cycloheximide action.

claims.claim: The non-rotated conformation protects 28–30 nt of mRNA.
claims.source: In either case, it is expected to trap the ribosome in a non-rotated conformation, suggesting that the non-rotated conformation protects 28–30 nt of mRNA.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the cycloheximide experiment results.

claims.claim: Anisomycin is an elongation inhibitor that binds to the peptidyl transferase center.
claims.source: We next conducted ribosome-profiling experiments using yeast treated with anisomycin, an elongation inhibitor that binds to the peptidyl transferase center (Grollman, 1967; Hansen et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Almost exclusively small footprints were observed in yeast treated with anisomycin.
claims.source: We observed almost exclusively small footprints in yeast treated with anisomycin (Figure 3D–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D-F.

claims.claim: Anisomycin stabilizes a distinct conformation of the ribosome that protects 20–22 nt of mRNA.
claims.source: By comparison to the effects of cycloheximide treatment, we inferred that anisomycin stabilizes a distinct conformation of the ribosome that protects 20–22 nt of mRNA.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of anisomycin and cycloheximide effects.

claims.claim: Anisomycin has higher affinity for post-translocation ribosomes than for pre-translocation, cycloheximide-treated ribosomes.
claims.source: Although anisomycin's precise mechanism is not characterized, it has higher affinity for post-translocation ribosomes than for pre-translocation, cycloheximide-treated ribosomes, suggesting that it preferentially binds a ribosome conformation distinct from that stabilized by cycloheximide (Barbacid and Vazquez, 1974, 1975).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Lincomycin and other antibiotics that bind the peptidyl transferase center induce translocation.
claims.source: Lincomycin and other antibiotics that bind the peptidyl transferase center induce translocation, and lincomycin-treated ribosomes prefer a rotated conformation in in vitro FRET experiments (Fredrick and Noller, 2003; Ermolenko et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Lincomycin-treated ribosomes prefer a rotated conformation in in vitro FRET experiments.
claims.source: Lincomycin and other antibiotics that bind the peptidyl transferase center induce translocation, and lincomycin-treated ribosomes prefer a rotated conformation in in vitro FRET experiments (Fredrick and Noller, 2003; Ermolenko et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: It is possible that anisomycin acts similarly to lincomycin to stabilize a rotated conformation.
claims.source: It is possible that anisomycin acts similarly to stabilize a rotated conformation.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the similarity to lincomycin's mechanism.

claims.claim: Two distinct ribosome conformations can be stabilized using elongation inhibitors.
claims.source: We have thus demonstrated that two distinct ribosome conformations can be stabilized using elongation inhibitors.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the differential effects of cycloheximide and anisomycin.

claims.claim: Stabilization of distinct conformations by two drugs resulted in a nearly complete reciprocal bias in the size of ribosome footprints.
claims.source: Stabilization of distinct conformations by two drugs resulted in a nearly complete reciprocal bias in the size of ribosome footprints, providing evidence that large and small footprints originate from distinct ribosomal conformations.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the experimental data with cycloheximide and anisomycin.

claims.claim: Large and small footprints originate from distinct ribosomal conformations.
claims.source: Stabilization of distinct conformations by two drugs resulted in a nearly complete reciprocal bias in the size of ribosome footprints, providing evidence that large and small footprints originate from distinct ribosomal conformations.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of elongation inhibitors.

claims.claim: Each ribosome cycles through both conformations, protecting first a large footprint and then a small footprint at each codon.
claims.source: We hypothesize that each ribosome cycles through both conformations, protecting first a large footprint and then a small footprint at each codon.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their data.

claims.claim: The ratio of large to small footprints in untreated cells could show, at single-codon resolution, how many ribosomes are in each stage of elongation.
claims.source: The footprints identified by high-throughput sequencing in a ribosome-profiling experiment represent a deep sampling of ribosomes in different states, and thus the ratio of large to small footprints in untreated cells could show, at single-codon resolution, how many ribosomes are in each stage of elongation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the interpretation of footprint data.

claims.claim: 3-amino-1,2,4-triazole (3-AT) is an inhibitor of histidine biosynthesis.
claims.source: We treated yeast with 3-amino-1,2,4-triazole (3-AT), an inhibitor of histidine biosynthesis, to create a specific shortage of His-acylated tRNA and cause ribosomes to pause on histidine codons (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about 3-AT.

claims.claim: Treatment with 3-AT creates a specific shortage of His-acylated tRNA and causes ribosomes to pause on histidine codons.
claims.source: We treated yeast with 3-amino-1,2,4-triazole (3-AT), an inhibitor of histidine biosynthesis, to create a specific shortage of His-acylated tRNA and cause ribosomes to pause on histidine codons (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the known mechanism of 3-AT action.

claims.claim: The shortage of His-tRNA dramatically increased the relative abundance of large footprints from ribosomes with His codons in the A site.
claims.source: We found that the shortage of His-tRNA dramatically increased the relative abundance of large footprints from ribosomes with His codons in the A site, with minimal effect on the abundance of small footprints (Figure 4B,C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The shortage of His-tRNA had minimal effect on the abundance of small footprints.
claims.source: We found that the shortage of His-tRNA dramatically increased the relative abundance of large footprints from ribosomes with His codons in the A site, with minimal effect on the abundance of small footprints (Figure 4B,C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: During the decoding phase of elongation, before peptide bond formation, the ribosome is in a non-rotated conformation.
claims.source: During the decoding phase of elongation, before peptide bond formation, the ribosome is in a non-rotated conformation (Frank and Agrawal, 2000; Gao et al., 2009); these results therefore strongly suggest that the decoding phase of elongation (the non-rotated conformation) is represented by large footprints.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claims.claim: The decoding phase of elongation (the non-rotated conformation) is represented by large footprints.
claims.source: During the decoding phase of elongation, before peptide bond formation, the ribosome is in a non-rotated conformation (Frank and Agrawal, 2000; Gao et al., 2009); these results therefore strongly suggest that the decoding phase of elongation (the non-rotated conformation) is represented by large footprints.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the 3-AT experiment results combined with knowledge of ribosome conformations.

claims.claim: Translation speed varies systematically by codon.
claims.source: Recently, ribosome profiling has revealed that translation speed varies systematically by codon (Tuller et al., 2010; Stadler and Fire, 2011; Dana and Tuller, 2012); we hypothesized that there might be distinct codon-specific effects on the rate of the two distinct phases of elongation represented by small and large footprints.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous ribosome profiling studies.

claims.claim: Small footprints ranged from 38 ± 12% (UUU) to 87 ± 9% (CGG) of the total footprints for a given codon identity, averaged across three replicates.
claims.source: We found substantial variation in the characteristic length distribution between codons: small footprints ranged from 38 ± 12% (UUU) to 87 ± 9% (CGG) of the total footprints for a given codon identity, averaged across three replicates.
claims.evidence: This is supported by per-codon analysis of footprint data.

claims.claim: The relative occupancies of codons varied over a fivefold range, from 0.48 ± 0.04 (GGU) to 2.6 ± 0.67 (CCG).
claims.source: The relative occupancies varied over a fivefold range, from 0.48 ± 0.04 (GGU) to 2.6 ± 0.67 (CCG) (unitless, average of three replicates) and were highly correlated between independent replicates (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by per-codon occupancy analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The relative occupancies were highly correlated between independent replicates.
claims.source: The relative occupancies varied over a fivefold range, from 0.48 ± 0.04 (GGU) to 2.6 ± 0.67 (CCG) (unitless, average of three replicates) and were highly correlated between independent replicates (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The range of occupancies relative to the codon in the A site was much broader than the range of occupancies relative to the next codon.
claims.source: We found that the range of occupancies relative to the codon in the A site was much broader than the range of occupancies relative to the next codon, suggesting that the A-site occupancies reflect an aspect of translation, not merely confounding factors such as biases in fragment capture (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of A-site and downstream codon occupancies.

claims.claim: The A-site occupancies reflect an aspect of translation, not merely confounding factors such as biases in fragment capture.
claims.source: We found that the range of occupancies relative to the codon in the A site was much broader than the range of occupancies relative to the next codon, suggesting that the A-site occupancies reflect an aspect of translation, not merely confounding factors such as biases in fragment capture (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of A-site and downstream codon occupancies.

claims.claim: Codon identity affected both the pre-peptide-bond and post-peptide-bond stages of elongation.
claims.source: As with overall occupancy, the relative abundances of small footprints and the relative abundance of large footprints were both highly correlated between replicates (Figure 5C,D). This suggests that codon identity affected both the pre-peptide-bond and post-peptide-bond stages of elongation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the reproducibility of codon-specific footprint abundances.

claims.claim: The codon-specific relative abundances of small and large footprints were almost uncorrelated (Spearman's r = 0.11, average of three replicates).
claims.source: However, the effect of codon identity on the inferred duration of these two phases of the elongation cycle was distinct: the codon-specific relative abundances of small and large footprints were almost uncorrelated (Spearman's r = 0.11, average of three replicates).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of footprint abundances.

claims.claim: A major determinant of the abundance of footprints from each conformation was the identity of the amino acid encoded by the A-site codon.
claims.source: We found that a major and unexpected determinant of the abundance of footprints from each conformation was the identity of the amino acid encoded by the A-site codon.
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of footprint abundance by amino acid identity.

claims.claim: There is a much greater density of small footprints at codons encoding smaller, polar amino acids than at codons encoding large, aromatic amino acids.
claims.source: We found a much greater density of small footprints at codons encoding smaller, polar amino acids than at codons encoding large, aromatic amino acids.
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of footprint abundance by amino acid properties.

claims.claim: The relative abundance of small footprints at codons encoding a given amino acid was correlated with measures of polarity of the cognate amino acid (Spearman's r = −0.75 when grouped by amino acid, r = −0.58 by codon).
claims.source: The relative abundance of small footprints at codons encoding a given amino acid was correlated with measures of polarity of the cognate amino acid, such as the Kd of transfer of side chains from vapor to water (Spearman's r = −0.75 when grouped by amino acid, r = −0.58 by codon, Figure 6A), while the relative abundance of large footprints showed no correlation to amino acid polarity (Spearman's r = 0.11 by amino acid, r = 0.02 by codon) (Wolfenden, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The relative abundance of large footprints showed no correlation to amino acid polarity (Spearman's r = 0.11 by amino acid, r = 0.02 by codon).
claims.source: The relative abundance of small footprints at codons encoding a given amino acid was correlated with measures of polarity of the cognate amino acid, such as the Kd of transfer of side chains from vapor to water (Spearman's r = −0.75 when grouped by amino acid, r = −0.58 by codon, Figure 6A), while the relative abundance of large footprints showed no correlation to amino acid polarity (Spearman's r = 0.11 by amino acid, r = 0.02 by codon) (Wolfenden, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claims.claim: The chemical properties of the amino acid specified by the codon in the A site affect the stability of the rotated, post-peptide-bond conformation of the ribosome.
claims.source: These data strongly suggest that the chemical properties of the amino acid specified by the codon in the A site affect the stability of the rotated, post-peptide-bond conformation of the ribosome.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between amino acid polarity and small footprint abundance.

claims.claim: Interactions between the ribosome and polar amino acids acylated to the A-site tRNA can slow translocation substantially.
claims.source: We hypothesize that interactions between the ribosome and polar amino acids acylated to the A-site tRNA can slow translocation substantially.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the polarity correlation.

claims.claim: In yeast, the number of genes encoding a specific tRNA has been shown to be highly correlated with both codon usage and cellular tRNA concentrations.
claims.source: In yeast, the number of genes encoding a specific tRNA has been shown to be highly correlated with both codon usage and cellular tRNA concentrations (Percudani et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claims.claim: The relative occupancy per codon was only weakly correlated with tAI (Spearman's r = −0.39, average of three replicates).
claims.source: We found that the relative occupancy per codon was only weakly correlated with tAI and with tRNA genomic copy number (Spearman's r = −0.39 and −0.28, respectively; average of three replicates) and that the tAI was not particularly correlated with the relative abundance of either small footprints or large footprints (r = −0.34 and r = −0.20, respectively; average of three replicates).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of occupancy and tAI.

claims.claim: The relative occupancy per codon was only weakly correlated with tRNA genomic copy number (Spearman's r = −0.28, average of three replicates).
claims.source: We found that the relative occupancy per codon was only weakly correlated with tAI and with tRNA genomic copy number (Spearman's r = −0.39 and −0.28, respectively; average of three replicates) and that the tAI was not particularly correlated with the relative abundance of either small footprints or large footprints (r = −0.34 and r = −0.20, respectively; average of three replicates).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of occupancy and tRNA copy number.

claims.claim: The tAI was not particularly correlated with the relative abundance of small footprints (r = −0.34, average of three replicates).
claims.source: We found that the relative occupancy per codon was only weakly correlated with tAI and with tRNA genomic copy number (Spearman's r = −0.39 and −0.28, respectively; average of three replicates) and that the tAI was not particularly correlated with the relative abundance of either small footprints or large footprints (r = −0.34 and r = −0.20, respectively; average of three replicates).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claims.claim: The tAI was not particularly correlated with the relative abundance of large footprints (r = −0.20, average of three replicates).
claims.source: We found that the relative occupancy per codon was only weakly correlated with tAI and with tRNA genomic copy number (Spearman's r = −0.39 and −0.28, respectively; average of three replicates) and that the tAI was not particularly correlated with the relative abundance of either small footprints or large footprints (r = −0.34 and r = −0.20, respectively; average of three replicates).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Codon 'optimality', as represented by the tAI, does not appear to be a major determinant of relative ribosome occupancy under the conditions tested.
claims.source: Thus, unexpectedly, codon 'optimality', as represented by the tAI, does not appear to be a major determinant of relative ribosome occupancy under the conditions tested here.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the weak correlations between tAI and occupancy measures.

claims.claim: In an extreme case, a limited supply of the tRNA cognate to the A-site codon slows translation during the large-footprint stage.
claims.source: The 3-AT data show that in an extreme case, a limited supply of the tRNA cognate to the A-site codon slows translation during the large-footprint stage.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the 3-AT experiment results.

claims.claim: The differences in abundance among tRNAs in wild-type cells have only a minor effect on relative ribosome occupancy of the cognate codons under optimum growth conditions.
claims.source: In contrast, our overall results in untreated yeast suggest that the differences in abundance among tRNAs in wild-type cells have only a minor effect on relative ribosome occupancy of the cognate codons under optimum growth conditions.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the weak correlation between tRNA abundance and occupancy in untreated cells.

claims.claim: Wobble base pairing at the A site has recently been linked with slowed elongation in humans and worms.
claims.source: Wobble base pairing at the A site has recently been linked with slowed elongation in humans and worms (Stadler and Fire, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claims.claim: There was no consistent trend toward increased occupancy at wobble-paired codons.
claims.source: While we found no consistent trend toward increased occupancy at wobble-paired codons, we observed notably higher occupancy on a subset of wobble-paired codons comprising proline CCG (G-U base pairing), leucine CUG (G-U), and arginine CGA (A-I) (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of wobble-paired codons shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: There was notably higher occupancy on proline CCG (G-U base pairing), leucine CUG (G-U), and arginine CGA (A-I) wobble-paired codons.
claims.source: While we found no consistent trend toward increased occupancy at wobble-paired codons, we observed notably higher occupancy on a subset of wobble-paired codons comprising proline CCG (G-U base pairing), leucine CUG (G-U), and arginine CGA (A-I) (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: For the three wobble codon outliers (CCG, CUG, CGA), there is a dramatic increase in short footprints, representing post-decoding stages of translation.
claims.source: For these three wobble codon outliers, we see a dramatic increase in short footprints, representing post-decoding stages of translation (Figure 6C,D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claims.claim: The arginine CGA codon is known to be a strong inhibitor of translation in yeast.
claims.source: The arginine CGA codon is known to be a strong inhibitor of translation in yeast, and its inhibitory effect is due more to wobble decoding than tRNA abundance and may include interactions after the initial decoding (Letzring et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claims.claim: The inhibitory effect of CGA is due more to wobble decoding than tRNA abundance and may include interactions after the initial decoding.
claims.source: The arginine CGA codon is known to be a strong inhibitor of translation in yeast, and its inhibitory effect is due more to wobble decoding than tRNA abundance and may include interactions after the initial decoding (Letzring et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claims.claim: CGA is one of the most slowly translated codons.
claims.source: Our data confirm that CGA is indeed one of the most slowly translated codons, and its high relative occupancy is due to increased abundance of small footprints, suggesting that its slow elongation is primarily due to a prolonged post-decoding stage.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the occupancy and footprint data for CGA.

claims.claim: The high relative occupancy of CGA is due to increased abundance of small footprints.
claims.source: Our data confirm that CGA is indeed one of the most slowly translated codons, and its high relative occupancy is due to increased abundance of small footprints, suggesting that its slow elongation is primarily due to a prolonged post-decoding stage.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the footprint data for CGA.

claims.claim: The slow elongation of CGA is primarily due to a prolonged post-decoding stage.
claims.source: Our data confirm that CGA is indeed one of the most slowly translated codons, and its high relative occupancy is due to increased abundance of small footprints, suggesting that its slow elongation is primarily due to a prolonged post-decoding stage.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the increased abundance of small footprints at CGA.

claims.claim: The abundance of footprints from each step of elongation was clearly affected by several distinct codon-specific features with sometimes synergistic and sometimes opposing effects.
claims.source: Overall, the abundance of footprints from each step of elongation was clearly affected by several distinct codon-specific features with sometimes synergistic and sometimes opposing effects.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the multiple factors affecting footprint distributions.

claims.claim: The small footprints were revealed only after cycloheximide was omitted from the experimental procedure.
claims.source: We were quite surprised to discover that the ribosome protects two different footprint sizes (28–30 nt and 20–22 nt), as the original ribosome-profiling experiments and nuclease protection assays only captured the longer footprints (Ingolia et al., 2009). The difference is explained by the experimental conditions: the small footprints were revealed only after we left out cycloheximide, a translation inhibitor commonly used to stabilize ribosomes on mRNA for ribosome profiling.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of experiments with and without cycloheximide.

claims.claim: Early study of ribosome pausing found that when cycloheximide was omitted, 20–24 nt footprints accumulated in addition to the larger footprints.
claims.source: Indeed, early study of ribosome pausing found that when cycloheximide was omitted, 20–24 nt footprints accumulated in addition to the larger footprints they saw from cycloheximide-treated ribosomes (Wolin and Walter, 1988).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claims.claim: In early studies, the small and large footprints had the same 5′ terminus and differed at the 3′ end.
claims.source: As in our own experiments, the small and large footprints they observed had the same 5′ terminus and differed at the 3′ end.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research and comparison to current data.

claims.claim: Large footprints originate from non-rotated ribosomes during the decoding stage before peptide bond formation.
claims.source: We propose that the two footprints sizes originate from two ribosome conformations corresponding to different stages of elongation: large footprints from non-rotated ribosomes during the decoding stage before peptide bond formation, and small footprints from rotated ribosomes during the translocation stage after peptide bond formation.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: Small footprints originate from rotated ribosomes during the translocation stage after peptide bond formation.
claims.source: We propose that the two footprints sizes originate from two ribosome conformations corresponding to different stages of elongation: large footprints from non-rotated ribosomes during the decoding stage before peptide bond formation, and small footprints from rotated ribosomes during the translocation stage after peptide bond formation.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: Crystal structures of rotated and non-rotated ribosomes show that mRNA accessibility is not likely to be dramatically different between the two conformations.
claims.source: As for the physical origin of the small and large mRNA fragments, crystal structures of rotated and non-rotated ribosomes show that mRNA accessibility is not likely to be dramatically different between the two conformations (Ben-Shem et al., 2010, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claims.claim: RNAse I may be small enough to penetrate into the mRNA entrance channel and cleave the mRNA just two nucleotides from the A site.
claims.source: RNAse I may be small enough to penetrate into the mRNA entrance channel and cleave the mRNA just two nucleotides from the A site.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of footprint generation.

claims.claim: The ribosome itself may be more susceptible to RNAse degradation in the rotated conformation, allowing ribosomal RNA cleavage that enables RNAse I to access the mRNA entrance channel, yielding a smaller mRNA footprint.
claims.source: Alternately, the ribosome itself may be more susceptible to RNAse degradation in the rotated conformation, allowing ribosomal RNA cleavage that in turn enables RNAse I to access the mRNA entrance channel, yielding a smaller mRNA footprint.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism of footprint generation.

claims.claim: Both small and large footprints have been observed in wheat germ extract treated with micrococcal nuclease.
claims.source: Importantly, however, both small and large footprints have also been observed in wheat germ extract treated with micrococcal nuclease, indicating that the two footprint sizes are neither species- nor nuclease-specific (Wolin and Walter, 1988).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claims.claim: The two footprint sizes are neither species- nor nuclease-specific.
claims.source: Importantly, however, both small and large footprints have also been observed in wheat germ extract treated with micrococcal nuclease, indicating that the two footprint sizes are neither species- nor nuclease-specific (Wolin and Walter, 1988).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from observations in different species and with different nucleases.

claims.claim: The relative abundance of large and small footprints reflects the relative duration of different stages of elongation at each codon.
claims.source: We hypothesize that the relative abundance of large and small footprints reflects the relative duration of different stages of elongation at each codon.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claims.claim: The estimated bulk elongation rate is 5.6 amino acids per second.
claims.source: Comparing our relative occupancy values to an estimated bulk elongation rate of 5.6 amino acids per second (Ingolia et al., 2011), our model would predict variation in average codon elongation time from as little as 0.08 s (GGU) to as much as 0.5 s (CCG).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claims.claim: The model predicts variation in average codon elongation time from as little as 0.08 s (GGU) to as much as 0.5 s (CCG).
claims.source: Comparing our relative occupancy values to an estimated bulk elongation rate of 5.6 amino acids per second (Ingolia et al., 2011), our model would predict variation in average codon elongation time from as little as 0.08 s (GGU) to as much as 0.5 s (CCG).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the relative occupancy data and bulk elongation rate.

claims.claim: Ribosome footprint data have inherent biases from ligation and other steps of the library preparation.
claims.source: Ribosome footprint data have inherent biases from ligation and other steps of the library preparation.
claims.evidence: This is a known limitation of the method.

claims.claim: The overall balance of small and large footprints varied between replicates.
claims.source: Further, the overall balance of small and large footprints varied between replicates, leaving open the question of which conformation is more populated in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claims.claim: The codon-specific variation in the ratio of small to large footprints was robust despite overall variability.
claims.source: Nonetheless, although the overall ratio of small to large footprints varied, the codon-specific variation in this ratio was robust.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the reproducibility of codon-specific patterns.

claims.claim: Ribosomes are depleted from the first 50 codons when yeast are harvested without inhibitors.
claims.source: Ribosomes are depleted from the first 50 codons when yeast are harvested by the procedure we used without inhibitors.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claims.claim: Elongation continues for around 10 s after initiation ceases during the harvest process.
claims.source: We interpret this as evidence that elongation continues for around 10 s after initiation ceases during the harvest process.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the depletion pattern at the 5' end of genes.

claims.claim: Different harvest methods had large effects on the precise footprint locations even when the overall translation per gene was highly reproducible.
claims.source: Different harvest methods had large effects on the precise footprint locations even when the overall translation per gene was highly reproducible (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from unpublished data.

claims.claim: The average occupancies per codon with and without cycloheximide were surprisingly uncorrelated (Spearman's r = 0.02).
claims.source: Similarly, the average occupancies per codon with and without cycloheximide were surprisingly uncorrelated (Spearman's r = 0.02, comparing the average of three untreated samples and the average of two cycloheximide-treated samples), though the total footprints per gene correlated quite well (Spearman's r = 0.97 between the average fpkm in three untreated samples and the average fpkm in two cycloheximide-treated samples).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of treated and untreated samples.

claims.claim: The total footprints per gene correlated quite well between cycloheximide-treated and untreated samples (Spearman's r = 0.97).
claims.source: Similarly, the average occupancies per codon with and without cycloheximide were surprisingly uncorrelated (Spearman's r = 0.02, comparing the average of three untreated samples and the average of two cycloheximide-treated samples), though the total footprints per gene correlated quite well (Spearman's r = 0.97 between the average fpkm in three untreated samples and the average fpkm in two cycloheximide-treated samples).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of treated and untreated samples.

claims.claim: Evolution has tuned tRNA sequence and modifications to balance the contributions of amino acid identity, codon pairing strength, and tRNA structure to binding affinity such that most aminoacylated tRNAs have similar affinity to ribosomal A sites.
claims.source: Biochemical evidence suggests that evolution has tuned tRNA sequence and modifications to balance the contributions of amino acid identity, codon pairing strength, and tRNA structure to binding affinity of a given tRNA, such that most aminoacylated tRNAs have similar affinity to ribosomal A sites (Olejniczak et al., 2005; Dale et al., 2009; Shepotinovskaya and Uhlenbeck, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous biochemical studies.

claims.claim: Ribosome profiling has revealed a lack of uniformity both in decoding and post-decoding steps.
claims.source: While this affinity tuning is a plausible result of selection for fidelity in decoding, ribosome profiling has revealed a lack of uniformity both in decoding and post-decoding steps.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the ribosome profiling data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The great diversity in physical properties of amino acids and in the intrinsic stability of the codon–anticodon interaction may lead to wide variation in the kinetics of post-decoding steps.
claims.source: Once the interactions that determine the codon-specific rate of decoding are decoupled and replaced by a new set of codon-specific interactions in the subsequent steps of elongation, the great diversity in physical properties of amino acids and in the intrinsic stability of the codon–anticodon interaction may lead to wide variation in the kinetics of post-decoding steps.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the mechanistic basis for observed variation.

results.result: Ribosome profiling reveals two distinct populations of ribosome footprints (28-30 nt and 20-22 nt) that represent ribosomes in distinct conformational states. Both footprint populations localize to coding sequences with 3-nucleotide periodicity, confirming they originate from translating ribosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C24-C27 provide strong experimental evidence from sequencing data showing two distinct footprint populations with appropriate localization and periodicity. Claims C5, C6, C22, and C23 are supported by differential effects of elongation inhibitors. The data in Figures 2 and 3 directly support these findings with multiple replicates.

results.result: Small and large footprints have the same 5' ends positioned 15-16 nt upstream of the A-site codon but differ at their 3' ends, with small footprints extending 2-3 nt beyond the A-site codon and large footprints extending 10 nt beyond.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30 are supported by metagene analysis shown in Figure 2F. The inference about footprint positioning relative to the A-site is based on established knowledge about start codon positioning and is consistent with the observed periodicity patterns.

results.result: Cycloheximide treatment stabilizes ribosomes in a non-rotated conformation that predominantly protects 28-30 nt footprints, with very few 20-22 nt footprints observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 are directly supported by experimental data in Figure 3A-C showing predominance of large footprints with cycloheximide. Claims C37-C39 combine cited prior knowledge about cycloheximide mechanism (C37) with reasonable inference about ribosome conformation (C38-C39). The interpretation is consistent with established understanding of cycloheximide action.

results.result: Anisomycin treatment stabilizes a distinct ribosome conformation that predominantly protects 20-22 nt footprints, likely representing a rotated conformation based on analogy to lincomycin.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 are strongly supported by experimental data in Figure 3D-F showing predominance of small footprints with anisomycin. Claim C43 is supported by cited prior work. Claims C44-C46 provide mechanistic context through analogy to lincomycin, though C46 acknowledges this is speculative. The reciprocal effects of cycloheximide and anisomycin provide strong evidence for distinct conformational states.

results.result: Two distinct ribosome conformations can be stabilized using elongation inhibitors, and the nearly complete reciprocal bias in footprint sizes between cycloheximide and anisomycin treatment provides evidence that large and small footprints originate from distinct ribosomal conformations.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 are well-supported by the combined experimental data from cycloheximide and anisomycin treatments shown in Figure 3. The reciprocal effects provide strong evidence for the interpretation that footprint size reflects conformational state.

results.result: Treatment with 3-AT creates histidine starvation that dramatically increases large footprints at histidine codons with minimal effect on small footprints, demonstrating that the decoding phase (non-rotated conformation) is represented by large footprints.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 are directly supported by experimental data in Figure 4. Claim C56 is supported by cited structural studies. Claim C57 represents a strong inference combining the 3-AT experimental results with established knowledge about ribosome conformations during decoding. This provides key evidence linking footprint size to specific elongation stages.

results.result: Substantial codon-specific variation exists in footprint distributions and relative occupancies, with small footprints ranging from 38±12% to 87±9% of total footprints and relative occupancies varying over a fivefold range. These patterns are highly reproducible between replicates and reflect aspects of translation rather than technical artifacts.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61 are directly supported by per-codon analysis shown in Figure 5. Claims C62-C63 provide important validation that the observed patterns reflect biological processes rather than technical biases, supported by comparison of A-site versus downstream codon occupancies.

results.result: Codon identity affects both pre-peptide-bond and post-peptide-bond stages of elongation, but the effects on these two phases are distinct, as evidenced by the near-zero correlation (r=0.11) between small and large footprint abundances across codons.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 are supported by correlation analysis of footprint data shown in Figure 5C-D. The reproducibility of codon-specific patterns combined with the lack of correlation between small and large footprint abundances provides strong evidence for distinct codon effects on different elongation stages.

results.result: Amino acid polarity is a major determinant of small footprint abundance, with small footprints more abundant at codons encoding polar amino acids (Spearman's r=-0.75 by amino acid), while large footprint abundance shows no correlation with polarity. This suggests amino acid properties affect the stability of the rotated, post-peptide-bond conformation.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 are directly supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6A. The strong correlation with polarity for small but not large footprints provides compelling evidence. Claim C70 represents a reasonable inference from this data, though the exact mechanism remains to be determined.

results.result: Codon optimality (tAI) and tRNA abundance show only weak correlations with relative occupancy and footprint abundances (r=-0.39 to -0.20), suggesting that tRNA availability is not a major determinant of ribosome occupancy under optimal growth conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76 are supported by correlation analysis of tAI and tRNA copy number with occupancy measures. Claims C77 and C79 represent reasonable inferences from these weak correlations. This finding is somewhat surprising but well-supported by the data, though it contrasts with the 3-AT experiment showing tRNA limitation can affect occupancy under extreme conditions.

results.result: While wobble pairing shows no consistent effect on occupancy, three specific wobble codons (CCG, CUG, CGA) show notably higher occupancy with dramatic increases in small footprints. The CGA codon shows particularly slow translation due to a prolonged post-decoding stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C83 are supported by data in Figure 6B-D. Claims C84-C85 are supported by cited prior work on CGA. Claims C86-C88 combine the current footprint data with prior knowledge to provide mechanistic insight into CGA's inhibitory effect. The interpretation that slow elongation at CGA is due to prolonged post-decoding is well-supported by the increased small footprints.

results.result: The authors propose a model where each ribosome cycles through both conformations at each codon, with large footprints originating from non-rotated ribosomes during decoding and small footprints from rotated ribosomes during translocation. The ratio of footprint sizes could reflect the relative duration of different elongation stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C50, C51, C93, C94, and C100 represent the authors' proposed model integrating their experimental findings. While these are explicitly stated as hypotheses/proposals, they are well-supported by the combined evidence from drug treatments (cycloheximide, anisomycin, 3-AT), codon-specific patterns, and consistency with established structural knowledge. The model provides a coherent framework explaining all major observations.

results.result: Small footprints were revealed only after omitting cycloheximide from the experimental procedure. Previous studies also observed both footprint sizes in the absence of cycloheximide, and both sizes have been observed with different nucleases and in different species, indicating the phenomenon is neither species- nor nuclease-specific.
results.evaluation: Claim C90 is supported by comparison of experiments with and without cycloheximide. Claims C91-C92 and C98-C99 are supported by citations to prior work (Wolin and Walter, 1988), providing important validation that the two footprint sizes are a general phenomenon rather than an artifact of the specific experimental conditions.

results.result: While ribosome footprint data have inherent technical biases and the overall balance of small and large footprints varied between replicates, the codon-specific variation in footprint ratios was robust and reproducible.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C105 acknowledge important limitations while highlighting the robustness of the key findings. The reproducibility of codon-specific patterns despite overall variability strengthens confidence in the biological significance of the observations.

results.result: Harvest methods significantly affect footprint distributions, with ribosomes depleted from the first 50 codons in untreated samples (suggesting ~10s of continued elongation after initiation ceases) and surprisingly low correlation of per-codon occupancies between cycloheximide-treated and untreated samples (r=0.02), though per-gene totals correlate well (r=0.97).
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C110 are supported by correlation analysis and observed depletion patterns. These findings highlight important methodological considerations and potential artifacts that must be considered when interpreting ribosome profiling data. The exclusion of the first 50 codons from analysis is appropriately justified.

results.result: Using an estimated bulk elongation rate of 5.6 amino acids per second, the model predicts codon-specific elongation times ranging from 0.08s (GGU) to 0.5s (CCG).
results.evaluation: Claim C101 cites a prior estimate of elongation rate. Claim C102 represents a calculation based on relative occupancy data and this rate estimate. However, the authors acknowledge multiple caveats about interpreting occupancy as duration, including technical biases and uncertainty about which conformation is more populated in vivo. The calculation is reasonable but should be considered preliminary.

results.result: The authors hypothesize that interactions between the ribosome and polar amino acids acylated to the A-site tRNA can slow translocation substantially.
results.evaluation: Claim C71 is explicitly stated as a hypothesis to explain the observed correlation between amino acid polarity and small footprint abundance. While the correlation is well-supported, the specific molecular mechanism remains speculative and would require additional biochemical or structural studies to validate.

results.result: The authors initially hypothesized that non-rotated and rotated ribosomes might protect different lengths of mRNA, and that the two footprint sizes might represent these two conformations.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 describe the initial hypothesis that motivated the drug treatment experiments. While stated as a hypothesis, it is subsequently well-supported by the experimental evidence from cycloheximide, anisomycin, and 3-AT treatments. This represents the conceptual framework that guided the experimental design.

results.result: Crystal structures suggest mRNA accessibility is not dramatically different between rotated and non-rotated conformations. The physical mechanism generating different footprint sizes may involve RNase I penetrating the mRNA entrance channel or differential ribosomal RNA susceptibility to degradation in different conformations.
results.evaluation: Claim C95 is supported by cited structural studies. Claims C96-C97 are explicitly speculative proposals about the molecular mechanism of differential footprint generation. These remain unresolved questions requiring further investigation, though the observation that both footprint sizes occur with different nucleases (C98) provides some constraints on possible mechanisms.

results.result: Background claims establishing prior knowledge about translation elongation, ribosome conformational changes, ribosome profiling methodology, and properties of specific codons and inhibitors.
results.evaluation: These claims represent established knowledge from prior work, supported by appropriate citations. They provide essential context for interpreting the novel findings but are not themselves new results from this study.

results.result: The 3-AT experiment demonstrates that in an extreme case of tRNA limitation, translation slows during the large-footprint (decoding) stage.
results.evaluation: Claim C78 is directly supported by the 3-AT experimental data showing increased large footprints at histidine codons. This provides important validation of the model linking footprint size to elongation stage, though it represents an extreme perturbation rather than normal physiological conditions.

results.result: The abundance of footprints from each elongation step is affected by multiple codon-specific features with sometimes synergistic and opposing effects. Ribosome profiling reveals lack of uniformity in both decoding and post-decoding steps, potentially due to diversity in amino acid properties and codon-anticodon stability affecting post-decoding kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claim C89 represents a summary inference from the multiple factors identified (amino acid polarity, wobble pairing, etc.). Claim C112 is supported by the ribosome profiling data. Claim C113 is speculative but represents reasonable interpretation of the mechanistic basis for observed variation, consistent with the data showing distinct effects on different elongation stages.
